passage:
Subject: My ankle (please read before Saturday)

Dear Nilesh Sir,

I need to tell you something I've been hiding. At practice this week I said my ankle felt fine. It didn't. When I landed from the long jump on Thursday, I felt a sharp twinge and nearly cried, but I pretended I just tripped.
I wanted to be back so badly. I was scared that if I said it still hurt, you'd think I was weak or pick someone else for Saturday.
But my mother saw me limping and said if I make it worse, I could be out for much longer. That frightened me more.
So I'm telling you the truth. Can I sit out Saturday and go back to the doctor first?

Sorry,
Vandana

qa.q: When did Vandana feel a sharp twinge?
qa.a: Vandana felt it on Thursday when landing from the long jump.

qa.q: What made Vandana want to hide the pain at first?
qa.a: Vandana was scared the coach would think Vandana was weak or pick someone else, and badly wanted to be back.

qa.q: What was the wise choice Vandana made, and why?
qa.a: Telling Nilesh Sir the truth and asking to see the doctor first, because hiding pain could make the injury worse.

qa.q: How might Nilesh Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Nilesh Sir would likely be glad Vandana spoke up, and more worried about the ankle than about Saturday's team.

grounding: It shows a teenager eager to return who hid pain and risked a worse injury, then chose honesty over fear of being thought weak.

passage:
Sarita, you asked why I missed the whole season. Okay. So last June I hurt my wrist bowling in the nets. The doctor said to rest it. After a while I felt better, sort of, and the inter-school final was coming. I didn't tell anyone it still hurt. I strapped it myself and bowled eight overs.
By the sixth over I could barely grip the ball. I kept smiling so Coach wouldn't take me off.
Next morning my wrist was twice the size. Back to the doctor, and this time it was much longer out.
When I finally told Coach, she said, "Ritu, I'd never think less of you for being honest. I'd think less of a plan that breaks my best bowler."
I wish I'd said it before the final.

qa.q: How many overs did Ritu bowl in the final?
Why did Ritu keep smiling during the sixth over?
qa.a: Ritu was afraid Coach would end the spell and wanted so badly to keep playing that Ritu hid the pain.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Hiding the pain made the injury worse and kept Ritu out longer; telling Coach and following the doctor's pace next time would help.

qa.q: How did Coach feel about Ritu's honesty?
qa.a: Coach valued it and said she would never think less of Ritu for being honest, only of a plan that breaks her best bowler.

grounding: It shows a teenager who hid pain to play again, made the injury worse, and learned that the coach would not have thought less of the player for being honest.
